about.title: Long Beach Car Accident Claims
about.longDescription: Long Beach moves a lot of traffic for a city of 474,140 people. Port trucks share Pacific Coast Highway with commuters, the I-405 carries drivers between Orange County and the Westside, and Atlantic Avenue and Long Beach Boulevard run the length of the city from the shoreline to the north side. In 2025, the most recent final crash year, Long Beach recorded 2,135 injury collisions, 3,123 people injured and 19 traffic deaths. Reported crashes here tend to cluster on Fridays between 5 p.m. and 7 p.m., when the workweek lets out. If one of those collisions involved you, the days that follow can feel disorganized. Medical bills arrive before the insurance adjuster calls back, and the adjuster's questions may sound friendlier than they are. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect you with an independent personal injury attorney who handles Long Beach car accident claims on contingency, meaning no fee unless there is a recovery. You describe what happened, and an attorney explains where your claim stands under California law.

whyChoose.title: Why Long Beach Drivers Use LawProactive

items.title: California's clock is shorter than it looks
items.desc: You generally have two years to file a car accident injury claim, but if a City of Long Beach vehicle, a county truck or a Caltrans road condition is involved, the window to give notice can shrink to six months. An attorney can sort out which deadline applies before it slips by.

items.title: Being partly at fault does not end your claim
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, so a driver who was, say, 30 percent responsible can still pursue the other 70 percent. There is also no statutory cap on non-economic damages like pain and lost enjoyment of life in an ordinary car accident case.

items.title: No fee unless there is a recovery
items.desc: Attorneys in our network work on contingency, and LawProactive itself never charges you anything. You can find out whether you have a claim without adding another bill to the pile.

items.question: The other driver's insurer wants a recorded statement. Should I give one?
items.answer: You are not required to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company, and it is usually wise to hold off until you have spoken with an attorney. Adjusters can use small inconsistencies or offhand remarks to argue you were more at fault than you were. Report the crash to your own insurer as your policy requires, but let a lawyer handle the other side.

items.question: I was hit on Pacific Coast Highway near the port trucks. Does that change my claim?
items.answer: It can. Crashes involving commercial trucks, ride-share vehicles or government vehicles often bring in additional insurance policies, different record-keeping rules and, in the case of public agencies, a much shorter notice deadline. An attorney can identify every responsible party and request driver logs or dashcam footage before it is overwritten.

items.question: What should I save after a Long Beach car accident?
items.answer: Keep the police report number, photos of both vehicles and the scene, the names of any witnesses, and every medical record and receipt, even for a rideshare to urgent care. Do not repair your car or delete phone photos until an attorney has reviewed them. Evidence from busy corridors like Long Beach Boulevard or Atlantic Avenue, including nearby business cameras, can disappear within days.
